items.summary: The updated KTM 200 Duke gets ride-by-wire, two ride modes, Crawl Assist and two new colours, with a price increase of Rs 1,552.
items.text: KTM has now officially launched the new 200 Duke in India. Priced at Rs 2,07,140 (ex-showroom Delhi), the motorcycle gains a significant electronics upgrade for a price increase of Rs 1,552. The biggest changes centre on the electronics package. KTM has introduced ride-by-wire throttle control, a bi-directional quickshifter, traction control and two ride modes as standard equipment on the 200 Duke. The quickshifter enables clutchless upshifts and downshifts, while Street and Rain modes allow riders to adapt power delivery to the conditions. Traction control helps manage rear-wheel traction. These functions can be accessed through the updated TFT instrument interface, which allows riders to manage the traction control, ride modes and quickshifter settings. The additions bring features associated with KTM’s larger motorcycles to its 200cc streetfighter. Another feature confirmed in the official announcement is Crawl Assist. KTM says it is intended to reduce rider fatigue in slow-moving, stop-and-go traffic. This adds a convenience-focused element to an update otherwise centred on performance and rider control. Its operation and effectiveness in everyday traffic will become clearer once we ride the updated motorcycle. KTM has introduced two new colours – Liquid Carbon and Slate Grey. items.title: Royal Enfield Classic 350 Spied With Tubeless Spoke Wheels – Launch Soon
items.summary: A Classic 350 in Medallion Bronze has spied at at dealership with a different spoke-wheel setup - finally getting tubeless option on best selling RE
items.text: After years of waiting, Royal Enfield could finally launch the much awaited practical update for the Classic 350, with spyshots from dealership showing the motorcycle equipped with what appears to be a tubeless-compatible spoke wheel. The Medallion Bronze Classic 350 retains its familiar retro design, but a closer look at the front wheel reveals a different rim and spoke attachment arrangement. The close-up images show a black-finished front rim with spokes attaching to a raised flange. This differs from the conventional arrangement in which spoke pass through the central section of the rim. The visible construction appears consistent with a design intended to accommodate tubeless tyres. The motorcycle otherwise retains familiar components, including its telescopic front fork, front disc brake with ByBre caliper and ABS sensor ring. The wheel design appears to resemble the tubeless spoke-wheel setup associated with the Meteor 350 Sundowner Edition, rather than the side-laced arrangement seen on the Goan Classic 350. For Classic buyers who prefer the appearance of spokes, such an option could remove one reason to choose alloy wheels. The main attraction is puncture-repair convenience. Many small tread punctures in a tubeless tyre can be temporarily plugged without removing the wheel, making roadside repairs more manageable. items.title: 2027 Kawasaki Z900 launched at Rs 9.99 lakh
items.summary: Kawasaki has launched the 2027 model year Z900 super-naked in India with two new colours as the only change. Tap to know more.
items.text: The Z900 got a comprehensive makeover for model year 2025, and Kawasaki has managed to keep the price at a rather sweet Rs 9.99 lakh despite the GST revision. For 2027, the brand is changing only the colour options offered and has left the motorcycle untouched, including the aforementioned ex-showroom price. To recap, Kawasaki refreshed the entire design of the Z900 in 2025 , giving it a sharper Sugomi styling and an enhanced suite of electronics. Some of these include a completely new 5-inch TFT display with smartphone connectivity, turn-by-turn navigation, cornering-sensitive ABS and traction control, and cruise control. All of that gets carried over to 2027, as does the 948cc inline-four liquid-cooled engine making 124hp at 9,500rpm and 98.6Nm at 7,700rpm. Other cycle parts remain unchanged as well, including the USD fork and backlink monoshock units, as well as front and rear brakes. The full electronics suite and the rebound- and spring-adjustable suspension at both ends have been carried over too. New for 2027 are the two colour options, white with a green frame and grey with a black frame. The model year 2026’s candy lime green with a grey frame and black with a gold frame options have been discontinued. Deliveries are expected to commence today. 2026 Kawasaki Z900 launched at Rs 9.99 lakh 2025 Kawasaki Z900 launched at Rs 9.52 lakh

items.text: Kawasaki India has updated the Z900 for 2027 model year at Rs 9.99 lakh ex-showroom. Now unlike the substantial overhaul that arrived with the previous update, this new MY27 motorcycle is largely a colour and homologation refresh. 2027 Z900 is now available in Ebony with Metallic Carbon Gray and Metallic Spark Black, and the awesome Pearl Blizzard White with Plasma Lime Green. Both these colourways are new to the India-spec motorcycle. The outgoing 2026 Z900 was offered in Metallic Matte Graphenesteel Gray with Metallic Flat Spark Black and Candy Lime Green with Metallic Carbon Gray. Both of which have now disappeared from Kawasaki India’s 2027 listing. There is, however, one small difference in the India-spec engine figures. The new Z900 continues with the 948cc liquid-cooled inline-four, but Kawasaki India now lists maximum output at 121bhp. For comparison, the official 2026 India page listed the same engine at 122bhp with identical torque output. That means the figure has fallen by 1bhp for MY27. Kawasaki has not explained the reason for this change. It could be related to homologation or the way the output is being declared for the latest model year. There is another small numerical difference. Kawasaki India now lists the 2027 Z900 at 213kg kerb, one kilogram heavier than the 212kg figure for the 2026 model. Estimated dry weight hence rises from 192kg to 193kg.

items.title: Bajaj Pulsar N250 2V Nears End as N250SS Takes Over
items.summary: Production of the older 2-valve Pulsar N250 has stopped and remaining motorcycles are expected to stay on sale only until dealer stocks run out.
items.text: Bajaj Pulsar N250 2V is nearing the end of its run in India with production of the existing motorcycle understood to have stopped. The outgoing model will continue to be available through dealerships until remaining inventory is exhausted after which the recently launched Pulsar N250SS will effectively take over the quarter-litre N-series position. Bajaj Auto has not yet issued an official discontinuation announcement for the older N250. The website continues to list the motorcycle at Rs 1,42,202, ex-showroom Delhi, with an active booking option. Customers may still find the older motorcycle at dealerships for some time depending on local inventory. The bigger clue comes from Bajaj’s own description of the newly launched Pulsar N250SS. The company calls it an “upgraded version of the Pulsar N250 ”, rather than positioning it as a separate derivative intended to sit permanently alongside the existing bike. The mechanical changes also make the replacement strategy fairly obvious. The outgoing Pulsar N250 uses a 249.07cc, single-cylinder, oil-cooled SOHC engine with two valves. It produces 24bhp and 21.5Nm and is paired with a five-speed gearbox. Pulsar N250SS takes that same basic quarter-litre idea considerably further. Its engine moves to a four-valve head and produces 24.5bhp and 22Nm. More importantly, Bajaj has replaced the five-speed transmission with a six-speed gearbox addressing one of the clearest limitations of the outgoing motorcycle.

items.title: Classic 350 with Tubeless Spoked Wheels Spotted
items.summary: The Classic 350 is currently offered with tubeless tyres only on alloy wheel variants.
items.text: Rejoice, avid Classic 350 owners and fans! Royal Enfield seems to be preparing a version of its popular retro cruiser with what appears to be cross-spoked rims. The demo unit on display at a dealership was seen with black powder-coated cross-spoke rims and CEAT tubeless tyres. Classic 350 has been offered with tube tyres on its spoked wheel variants for as long as the model has been on sale, while tubeless tyres have only been available with variants that feature alloy wheels. This meant that historically, buyers would have to choose between the convenience of, and lower maintenance with, tubeless tyres, or the style and charm of old-school spokes and tubes. Tubeless tyres offer several advantages over tube-type tyres. Tubeless tyres hold air pressure within the tyre itself, which seals against the tyre's bead. This means punctures encountered with tubeless tyres are safer, since the tyre loses pressure more gradually, rather than all at once. Moreover, these punctures are easier to patch since there is no inner tube, so neither the wheel nor the tyre has to be removed from the motorcycle. It remains to be seen whether Royal Enfield will release this in a standalone variant, or whether RE plans to retire tubed tyres from their range entirely. Regardless of how the automaker plans to roll it out, these cross-spoke wheels should be available for purchase as an add-on accessory that existing owners can also benefit from. items.title: Upcoming 2027 Honda CBR1000RR-R Spotted Testing
items.summary: The upcoming 2027 Honda CBR1000RR has been spotted testing abroad. The bike has undergone some important changes, including the addition of new brake calipers and some improvements to its aero.
items.text: Honda has started testing the upcoming 2027 CBR1000RR-R abroad, at the Jerez Circuit in Spain. It was ridden by Jonathan Rea, and images of the motorcycle were shared on his social media profile. The bike being tested right after the last round of the 2026 WorldSBK signals that the brand has some big plans for the 2027 WorldSBK. The bike has seen some changes, with the aeros being revised. At the front, the winglets have been enlarged for better downforce. In addition to this, the brand has also added ground effect pods, likely inspired by the Ducati Panigale V4 . These pods should improve the bike’s cornering speed, thus helping to improve lap times. Another interesting change is that the test mule was spotted with a differently shaped ram air intake compared to the current WorldSBK CBR1000RR-R. The reworked ram-air intake could have resulted in an improvement in performance. For reference, the current CBR1000RR-R is powered by a 999cc, liquid-cooled, inline-four engine that produces 217.5bhp at 14,000rpm and 113Nm at 12,000rpm. With the changes in regulations, we can expect the bike’s chassis to have received some tweaks. However, it is not clearly visible just going by the images shared online. Lastly, the brakes have been changed, with the test mule sporting Brembo callipers instead of the Nissin callipers. The change is likely due to Brembo being the new exclusive supplier of braking hardware for 2027 WorldSBK.

In a formal regulatory communication submitted to Indian stock exchanges, Schaeffler India disclosed that its promoter group entities—Schaeffler Schweinfurt Beteiligungs GmbH, Schaeffler Bühl Verwaltungs GmbH, Schaeffler Verwaltungsholding Sechs GmbH, and Industriewerk Schaeffler INA-Ingenieurdienst GmbH—are reviewing their equity holdings in the domestic unit. The promoter group currently holds a combined 74.13 percent stake in the paid-up share capital of Schaeffler India. The promoter group affirmed its intent to remain the controlling shareholder in the company, clarifying that any potential divestment would preserve its dominant shareholding position. "The Promoter Group continues to review its shareholding in the Company and may consider monetizing a small part of the same," Schaeffler AG noted in its communication to the board of directors of Schaeffler India. "The Promoter Group expresses its strong intention to continue as the significant majority shareholder block of the Company, representing at least two-thirds of the Company's shares outstanding."

items.title: Centre Allows E100 Ethanol Fuel For Compatible Flex-Fuel Vehicles
items.summary: The Centre has approved E100 ethanol fuel for compatible flex-fuel vehicles. Here
items.text: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules (CMVR), 1989, to permit the use of ethanol concentrations of up to E100 in compatible flex-fuel vehicles (FFVs). The amendment, notified through a gazette notification, expands the existing framework that includes E85 and is aimed at encouraging the adoption of vehicles capable of running on higher ethanol blends. The move is part of India’s broader efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, lower emissions and support the agricultural sector. Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari has also highlighted the potential benefits of ethanol blending for farmers. However, the latest notification does not, by itself, establish a transition plan for vehicles already on Indian roads that are designed to run on lower ethanol blends. E100 Approval Brings Existing Vehicle Compatibility into Focus Vehicles designed for ethanol blends above E20 require fuel system components and engine calibration suited to higher ethanol concentrations. Consequently, vehicles developed specifically for E20 fuel cannot be assumed to be compatible with E85 or E100. This distinction is important as India expands its ethanol fuel framework. While the latest amendment provides a regulatory pathway for compatible FFVs to use higher blends, questions remain about the long-term fuel options available to owners of vehicles designed for E20 or lower blends. Bigger engines, bigger fuel tanks, bigger price tags, and a bigger footprint usually signal a better bike, at least in the showroom. However, owning and living with one is a different story altogether. Heavyweight cruisers may be attractive to enthusiasts, but they are hard to maneuver, expensive to maintain, and tiring to ride in everyday conditions. This is where the middleweight cruisers shine. Middleweight cruisers combine the road presence of a big bike without the fuss of living with one. These cruisers come with an accessible price tag, just enough performance, and the convenience of an everyday motorcycle. A heavyweight cruiser is easy to fall for: massive road presence , premium build quality and materials, and big rumbling engines. However, the sticker price for one of these often runs well into five figures, and that is before insurance, accessories, and maintenance enter the picture. All these aspects that attracted you to buy a big cruiser are the actual cause of the fuss. Middleweight cruisers fix most of these issues without giving up on the good parts. You get a smaller engine with ample performance, lower running costs, and a footprint that is still substantial. These cruisers are lighter than heavyweights, so riding around town or maneuvering the bike in tight spaces is much easier. There’s one sound every motorcyclist dreads. You’re all kitted up, ready for a ride, you press the starter and… click. Nothing. The battery has given up before the ride has even begun. If you’ve got more than one bike, keeping batteries healthy can become a bit of a juggling act. Some bikes get used regularly, others sit for weeks, and modern electronics can quietly nibble away at the charge. Leave a battery discharged for too long and it may never properly recover. Replacement batteries aren’t cheap, either. Which brings me to Oxford’s new Oximiser Pro 5000. I’ve been testing one and, even at this early stage, I reckon Oxford has produced the battery charger that others will be judged against. That might sound like a big claim for something that lives in the garage, but this is a lot cleverer than simply pumping electricity into a battery. The Oximiser Pro range is designed to analyse a battery, charge it in controlled stages and then maintain it while the vehicle is parked. accessories.text: There’s something special about breaking away from your routine and heading out for a weekend ride. You might not want to spend the day revving the engine out and chasing apexes. Instead, you want enough grunt for confident overtaking, strong pulling power for those long highway stretches, and an engine with a bit of character. A distinctive exhaust note certainly wouldn’t hurt either. And for decades, American motorcycling has had a particular engine configuration that fits the bill rather well. What exactly does American touring require? Broadly, three things: enough grunt for confident overtaking, relaxed power delivery for long highway stretches, and comfort over hours in the saddle. Large-displacement V-twins, like those commonly found in American touring motorcycles , are well suited to the first two. They deliver plenty of torque at relatively low engine speeds, so you can roll on the throttle for an overtake without constantly working the gearbox or chasing the revs. It's worth pointing out, though, that we're talking about a particular application of the V-twin, not claiming every engine with this configuration behaves the same way. Ducati's L-twins , for instance, have powered everything from sporty road bikes to superbikes, showing just how differently the same basic layout can be tuned.
